posts.summary: SemiAnalysis 称 Anthropic 研究员用 Claude 找到了黎曼猜想的 Lean 证明，若验证通过将是 AI 数学能力的里程碑。
posts.text:
🚨🚨🚨ANOTHER MILLENNIUM PRIZE PROBLEM HAS BEEN CLAIMED🚨🚨🚨

Mathematician @__alpoge__  of @AnthropicAI claims that he used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, arguably the most significant open problem in mathematics.

Experts are still verifying the released Lean proof, but it seems very likely correct.

We estimate the output tokens alone would cost $44k at Fable 5.2 API prices, with plausible estimates for the total cost running in the millions. (1/4)🧵
posts.viewpoint: AI 推理能力的外溢值得关注，但短期与股票基本面关系有限。
posts.note: 跟踪证明验证进度与推理算力成本；非直接持仓信号。

posts.summary: 该证明包含约 2.5 亿页的“书”和 1740 万行 Lean 证明，估算仅输出 token 成本就约 4.4 万美元。
posts.text:
The proof comprises two artifacts: a “book” that Alpöge has not released because it is “slop,” spanning 250k+ pages, and a Lean proof of 17.4M lines that is the current object of discussion.

We can estimate the number of tokens in the book based on Levent’s previous papers on arXiv, which average 1,946 tokens in the TeX source per page of output PDF using Anthropic’s newest tokenizer. This implies roughly 487M output tokens.

A randomly sampled 1.5% of the Lean averaged 35 tokens per line, which implies roughly 610M output tokens.

At Fable 5.2’s current price of $40/million output tokens, this comes out to $44k. (2/4)
posts.viewpoint: 长上下文与推理成本是 AI 能力落地的隐性约束。
posts.note: 关注 token 成本与验证算力。

posts.summary: Alea 指出 AI 挤占 PCB/光子产能，汽车、工业、医疗等交期拉长，短缺可能持续到 2028 年；亚马逊等云厂已提前锁定供应。
posts.text:
I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.
posts.viewpoint: AI 供应链瓶颈从芯片扩散到 PCB/光模块，二线供应商有弹性。
posts.note: 跟踪 PCB、光模块、连接器与云厂锁产能。

posts.text: This conference season, Ayar Labs put real manufacturing statistics on its SuperNova ELSFPs. More than 100 laser units were measured at 50 C with -20 dB back reflections to simulate imperfections in fiber connectors and fiber-to-PIC coupling. The notable stats include a mean RIN of -158 dB/Hz and an especially low mean linewidth of 0.16 MHz, comparable to what 400ZR coherent class lasers are specified at; giving a lot of margin for DWDM operation. Importantly, every laser met spec with margin, which matters a lot more in production than one device achieving extraordinary performance.

posts.summary: Omercheema 用苏联面包供应故事类比计划经济与市场竞争，强调价格信号与分散决策。
posts.text:
In 1990s, shortly after the Soviet Union collapsed, a Russian official responsible for bread production visited London. Standing in shops stocked with fresh loaves of every variety, he asked his British hosts: who was in charge of the bread supply for the entire city?

The answer “nobody” left him stunned. In the Soviet Union,  Prices were fixed by the state, production was planned by committees, and shortages were managed through queues and rationing. Officials spent endless hours calculating how many loaves should be baked each day, yet the result was frequently too little, too much, or the wrong kind. 

In London there was no central bakery directorate, no daily conference of factory managers reporting to a ministry, and no price controls on the staple. Farmers, millers, bakers, and retailers simply competed. Each sought a profit; none coordinated by decree. The outcome was abundant, varied, and relatively inexpensive bread available on demand. The official could not immediately accept that this unplanned coordination, driven by price signals rather than commands, had solved a problem that central planning had never mastered.

Capitalism works. Healthy competition works. Unhealthy barriers to competition don't.
posts.viewpoint: 宏观叙事，但缺少直接市场信号。
posts.note: 低优先级；可作为长期框架。

posts.summary: Freda 解读腾讯/中国云厂对 AI capex 的口径：2026-27 见顶、之后资本开支强度下降；若行业 AI capex 正常化到 1 万亿美元以下，半导体可寻址市场将收缩。
posts.text:
$Tencent / Chinese CSPs’ tone on the AI capex cycle is very clear - 

Martin Lau laid out a clear case for why AI capex should moderate after 2027:

1/ Front-loaded investment: AI infrastructure is like building a factory. Once built, it can continuously train new models and generate tokens.

2/ Lower hardware costs: The same equipment should cost significantly less by 2028.

3/ Rapid efficiency gains: The same infrastructure can deliver exponentially more training compute and token output over time.

Takeaway: Martin is effectively calling for a peak in AI capex in 2026-27, with a meaningful decline in capex intensity thereafter, even as AI demand continues to grow.

The read-through for semis is interesting: If annual industry AI capex eventually normalizes below $1T, assigning a mid-range multiple to normalized earnings, that’s your industry total size.
posts.viewpoint: 中国云厂 capex 见顶是半导体需求侧的潜在拐点。

posts.summary: Ryan 长文讨论 post-training 推理需求：闭源推理需求仍强、开源推理增速更快，CSP 渠道反馈 2-3 年算力仍供不应求；核心风险是云厂 GW 收入能否维持。
posts.text:
我昨天指"Post-training是下一波算力浪潮"引起了范總和金老師的辯論。我就無意跟任何人辯論了，只是思考了一天，有空就想說下我都想法。

范兄說的話有道理。他指Post-trained開源推理模型小、Token成本小、收集優質data和eval進度慢，所以Post-trained模型帶來的算力和進度也不會很快(應該是和之前AI coding增長相比)。

確實如此，開源推理模型市場本身真的很小，收入只佔總體模型收入的幾%。所以即使開源有明顯增長，可能未來一年都不會為整體算力帶來明顯的增長。而且不能忽視優質data和eval等瓶頸。

我的看法是
1. 不只開源推理需求在上升，閉源推理需求也上升（增速變慢是確定的）。閉源推理需求很大程度上來自資深工程師、研究員、量化交易員、...等人的需求。對於這部分人來說，支付更多金錢從來不是問題，問題出在模型能力還不夠強，有不低的錯誤率和需要人工 review。模型還在進步當中，所以閉源推理需求上升是確定的。

2. Post-trained開源推理模型增速高於閉源推理增速，這是企業應用AI在workflow的關鍵。當workflow產生又同時帶動非傳統coding更複雜的AI需求(例如code review、security、testing、product design、 ...)

3. 很多人非常看重ROI，但很多公司都不是看ROI，而是看有沒有被新玩家顛覆的風險， token spending作用風險管理策略。

所以未來需求還是會大幅增長，問題從來是需求增速下降會不會導致供大於需。以我找到CSP的渠道，他們有信心2-3年算力繼續供不應求。即使需求增速變慢，供應依然是瓶頸。

對我來說唯一問題是雲能不能維持 >$ 50B/GW以上的暴利收入。我看法是GW收入不一定維持，但是整體半導體和算力依然供不應求。

范兄認為算力和半導體是週期性(下跌)的，長期看好AI，我表示尊重。我認為或許只有部分半導體公司的需求會面臨週期性下跌，會繼續缺貨的還是會繼續缺貨。
posts.viewpoint: 推理需求是下一波算力主线，供给瓶颈仍未缓解。
posts.note: 高优先级；跟踪 CSP capex、推理 token 与 GPU 租金。

posts.summary: Freda 与 50 位机器人前沿人士交流后给出 10 条判断：Astra 是机器人“GPT-3 时刻”，前沿实验室正把机器人变成新垂直领域。
posts.text:
10 Spicy Takes After Talking to 50 Friends at the Frontier of Robotics 🤖🔥

1/ Astra IS robotics' GPT-3 moment. Ironically, now that it's finally here, some in robotics seem reluctant to acknowledge it. Perhaps because it (sadly) didn't come from a robotics company?

2/ Robotics is becoming just another vertical for frontier labs. Not so different from coding in some respects. Why reinvent general intelligence for every industry?

3/ Robotics was too hard to underwrite until now. No convincing pretraining scaling law, no convergence on models, data, or hardware. No wonder some critics dismissed it as a fragmented industry playing an expensive "demo game". Astra may finally offer a credible path to scale.

4/ Robotics foundation-model startups have a case. But how strong is it? The argument: Astra handles System 2 (reasoning), while specialized models retain System 1 (skills) and System 0 (motor control). Fair. But isn't that already a narrower value proposition? And who says the boundary stops there?

5/ Follow the talent. Word is OpenAI reorganized its 30–40-person robotics team around the core Astra model. Hearing similar moves toward general models at @Tesla_Optimus. Org charts may tell us more than any demo.

6/ The robotics data gold rush is real. Million-hour procurement programs, some potentially reaching tens of millions of hours. Talk of budgets approaching $1B per frontier lab.

7/ Bullish on robotics hardware volumes. As intelligence becomes more accessible, the barriers to building useful robots could fall dramatically. The moat shifts toward reliability, dexterity, integration, and deployment.

8/ Robotics could fuel the next semiconductor and memory supercycle. A 100B-parameter model running on the edge requires ~50GB just for 4-bit weights. Now multiply that by millions of robots. Why do you think @JensenHuang is so obsessed with robotics? @elonmusk saw it coming: https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2114772074438988256?a=ZJpCuCM8Iv8RkRR_g_A&s=20

9/ Is self-driving immune to the general-model threat? After coding and robotics, why assume self-driving remains the exclusive domain of proprietary, vertical models? Robotaxi increasingly feels like a solved problem to me. But if and when frontier labs move into self-driving, we could see an Apple vs. Android dynamic. Think about the implications for $TSLA, Waymo, and other OEMs.

10/ The next bottleneck may not be intelligence. It's deployment. Models are improving faster than our ability to deploy robots in the messy real world. Integration, hardware variance, failure recovery, and economics remain brutally hard. The real moat may be turning intelligence into reliable, profitable physical work.

--
I realize some of these takes may rub people the wrong way, especially those who have spent years doing the hard work of advancing robotics. That's not my intention. 

I'm sharing them to spark debate, not to declare winners and losers. Astra has only been out for a month or so, and it's far too early to draw definitive conclusions. More importantly, when the TAM is this enormous - potentially the largest in tech - there should be plenty of room for different approaches and many winners.

++
Full diligence report: https://robonomics.substack.com/p/robotics-new-era-after-astra?r=3hcp4&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web

posts.text:
I’ll spell it out explicitly one last time. 

Everyone thinks Trump wants balanced trade. He does not. 

He wants to force allies to stop trading with China.  Completely. Zero inbound supply.  

Because it’s not just because of American jobs.  It’s a proactive move to slow down Chinas industrial rise. 

Everything is downstream of this.  Reserve currency status. The ability to address fiscal debt.  

It’s a crazy risk because China has a vote. 

It’s a crazy risk because you are forcing Europe to commit seppeku because they have very little leverage or say in the matter.   

It’s a crazy risk because Xi might bomb the fabs in Taiwan and the world doesn’t get AGI. 

It’s a crazy risk because China knows how financialized we are and will dump bonds and equities to drive anger towards trump.  

But it also has benefits if it works.  

If your allies can’t trade with China there is no near peer competitor to worry about. 

That has a ton of benefits. Just look at what happened after WW2/USSR collapse when American was the last man standing. 

Hegemony. 

Trumps advisors like Miran believe that you can coerce your allies to pay for your security umbrella in the form of buying longer dated treasuries. 

This removes the overhangs of the debt load while allowing you to pump markets in time for midterms.   

If Mexico can’t import from China then you solved the fentanyl crisis because they won’t have precursors. 

More importantly by establishing a tolerance for risk the level of fear you can instill in cartels is an order of magnitude higher.  

“Shit if they risked WW3 they won’t think twice about droning Sinaloa. “

This same “logic” applies to the Middle East.  

Now I will repeat for the 100x that this is not advocacy.  

I’m only telling you guys what the people in power believe.  And I’m telling you that what happens next if I’m right will come down to how Xi wants to fight.  

He can go gloves off or glove on.  There are real constraints as I have outlined in prior tweets.  

But there is a plan and therefore the tolerance for market pain is way way higher than you think.  

Because first you need Europe to be willing to commit economic seppuku. And they won’t want to (rightly). So Trump will crush them economically until they cry uncle.  And then they still won’t want to and he’s going to threaten to defang NATO.  And then they still won’t want to and he will withdraw swap lines. 

Or a lot more likely, he will do it all very forcefully and all at once to maximize leverage.  

Now you’ll rightly ask… why wasn’t this messaged better? Why have midwits like Lutnik on the team? 

Because you are attempting to execute a reckless gambit where the big variables are not what the tariffs rates are. Or if you tariff penguins.  Or if the person sounds dumb on TV. Non of that matters.  

What matters is - will Japan capitulate quickly and agree to buy a large amount of treasuries? Will Saudi capitulate quickly with your B2 bombers waiting in Diego Garcia to bomb Iran? Will China invade Taiwan?  

Many of you think everyone around Trump is retarded. I get it.  You hate the guy and everything he stands for.  But I will say this until I’m blue in the face.  Bessant, and even Miran, have higher IQs than most if not all of you. They thought through the second order effects.  Believe me.  If I, a dumb TMT L/S bro thought this far ahead, they certainly did too. Which means they warned Trump how risky this was and how deeply irrational it is if you planned to eventually cut a deal with China.  Therefore you have to assume Trump heard the risks and said “fuck it we ball” anyways.  

Economic Blitzkrieg.  That’s what we’re seeing.  And it’s only the start.
